section.heading: 6.3 Orthogonal Projections
section.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of a point in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ onto a line through the origin has an important analogue in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Given a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ and a subspace $$W$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , there is a vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in $$W$$ such that (1) $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the unique vector in $$W$$ for which $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$W$$ , and (2) $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the unique vector in $$W$$ closest to $$\textbf{y}$$ . See Figure 1. These two properties of $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ provide the key to finding least-squares solutions of linear systems.

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with two vectors projecting from point 0 on the plane in the form of a right-angled triangle.

section.paragraph: To prepare for the first theorem, observe that whenever a vector $$\textbf{y}$$ is written as a linear combination of vectors $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{n}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the terms in the sum for $$\textbf{y}$$ can be grouped into two parts so that $$\textbf{y}$$ can be written as
$$\textbf{y} = \textbf{z}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{2}$$

where $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of some of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ and $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is a linear combination of the rest of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ . This idea is particularly useful when $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{n} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis. Recall from Section 6.1 that $$W^{\bot}$$ denotes the set of all vectors orthogonal to a subspace $$W$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{u}_{5} \right\}$$ be an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ and let
$$\textbf{y} = c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5}$$

Consider the subspace $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , and write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of a vector $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ in $$W$$ and a vector $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ in $$W^{\bot}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Write

$$\mathbf{y} = \underset{\mathbf{z}_{1}}{\underset{︸}{c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{u}_{2}}} + \underset{\mathbf{z}_{2}}{\underset{︸}{c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5}}}$$
where $$\textbf{z}_{1} = c_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{u}_{2} \text{is in Span} \left{\right. \textbf{u}_{1} , \textbf{u}_{2} \left.\right}$$
and $$\textbf{z}_{2} = c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \text{is in Span} \left{\right. \textbf{u}_{3} , \textbf{u}_{4} , \textbf{u}_{5} \left.\right} .$$

To show that $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ , it suffices to show that $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is orthogonal to the vectors in the basis $$\left\{ \textbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \textbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ for $$W$$ . (See Section 6.1.) Using properties of the inner product, compute

$$\textbf{z}_{2} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & \left(\right. c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \left.\right) \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & c_{3} \textbf{u}_{3} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{4} \textbf{u}_{4} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} + c_{5} \textbf{u}_{5} \cdot \textbf{u}_{1} & = & 0$$

because $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ is orthogonal to $$\textbf{u}_{3}$$ , $$\textbf{u}_{4}$$ , and $$\textbf{u}_{5}$$ . A similar calculation shows that $$\textbf{z}_{2} \cdot \textbf{u}_{2} = 0$$ . Thus $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .

section.paragraph: The next theorem shows that the decomposition $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{z}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{2}$$ in Example 1 can be computed without having an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . It is enough to have an orthogonal basis only for $$W$$ .

note.heading: Theorem 8

note.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Then each $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ can be written uniquely in the form

section.paragraph: The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in (2) is called the orthogonal projection of y onto $$W$$ and often is written as $$\text{proj} _{W}{\textbf{y}}$$ . See Figure 2. When $$W$$ is a one-dimensional subspace, the formula for $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ matches the formula given in Section 6.2.
section.heading: Figure 2
section.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ ﻿onto $$W$$

image.alt: A figure shows a horizontal plane W with three vectors projecting from point 0 on the plane.

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Let $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ be any orthogonal basis for $$W$$ , and define $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ by (2).1 Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$W$$ because $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is a linear combination of the basis $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ . Let $$\textbf{z} = \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . Since $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}$$ , it follows from ( $$2$$ ) that

$$\left(\textbf{z} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} = ( \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} ) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} & = & \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} - \left(\frac{\textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u}_{1}}{\textbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}\right) \mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1} - 0 - \hdots - 0 & = & \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} - \left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{1} = 0$$

Thus $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ . Similarly, $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to each $$\mathbf{u}_{j}$$ in the basis for $$W$$ . Hence $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to every vector in $$W$$ . That is, $$\textbf{z}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ .

To show that the decomposition in (1) is unique, suppose $$\textbf{y}$$ can also be written as $$\textbf{y} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$$ , with $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ in $$W$$ and $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ in $$W^{\bot}$$ . Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} + \textbf{z} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{1}$$ (since both sides equal $$\textbf{y}$$ ), and so
$$\hat{\textbf{y}} - \left(\hat{\textbf{y}}\right)_{1} = \textbf{z}_{1} - \textbf{z}$$

This equality shows that the vector $$\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}} - {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ is in $$W$$ and in $$W^{\bot}$$ (because $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{z}$$ are both in $$W^{\bot}$$ , and $$W^{\bot}$$ is a subspace). Hence $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$$ , which shows that $$\mathbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ . This proves that $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = {\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ and also $$\textbf{z}_{1} = \textbf{z}$$ .
The uniqueness of the decomposition (1) shows that the orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ depends only on $$W$$ and not on the particular basis used in (2).

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 5 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Observe that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ . Write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of a vector in $$W$$ and a vector orthogonal to $$W$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ is

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\left(\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}\right)_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & \frac{9}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{3}{6} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \frac{9}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 5 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{15}{30} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 2 / 5 \\ 2 \\ 1 / 5\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Also
$$\textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} = \left[\right. 1 2 3 \left]\right. - \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 7 / 5 0 14 / 5 \left]\right.$$

Theorem 8 ensures that $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ . To check the calculations, however, it is a good idea to verify that $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ and hence to all of $$W$$ . The desired decomposition of $$\textbf{y}$$ is
$$\textbf{y} = \left[\right. 1 2 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right. + \left[\right. 7 / 5 0 14 / 5 \left]\right.$$

section.heading: A Geometric Interpretation of the Orthogonal Projection
section.paragraph: When $$W$$ is a one-dimensional subspace, the formula (2) for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ contains just one term. Thus, when $$\dim W > 1$$ , each term in (2) is itself an orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto a one-dimensional subspace spanned by one of the $$\mathbf{u}’s$$ in the basis for $$W$$ . Figure 3 illustrates this when $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . Here $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{1}$$ and $${\widehat{\textbf{y}}}_{2}$$ denote the projections of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto the lines spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , respectively. The orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ is the sum of the projections of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto one-dimensional subspaces that are orthogonal to each other. The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in Figure 3 corresponds to the vector $$\textbf{y}$$ in Figure 4 of Section 6.2, because now it is $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ that is in $$W$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows the orthogonal projection of y with mutually orthogonal subspaces on a three-dimensional axis.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The orthogonal projection of y ﻿is the sum of its projections onto one-dimensional subspaces that are mutually orthogonal

section.heading: Properties of Orthogonal Projections
section.paragraph: If $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ and if $$\textbf{y}$$ happens to be in $$W$$ , then the formula for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is exactly the same as the representation of $$\textbf{y}$$ given in Theorem 5 in Section 6.2. In this case, $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$$ .
This fact also follows from the next theorem.

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
T﻿he Best Approximation Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , let $$\textbf{y}$$ be any vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and let $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ be the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ . Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ , in the sense that

section.paragraph: The vector $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ in Theorem 9 is called the best approximation to $$\mathbf{y}$$ by elements of $$W$$ . Later sections in the text will examine problems where a given $$\textbf{y}$$ must be replaced, or approximated, by a vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ in some fixed subspace $$W$$ . The distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$\mathbf{v}$$ , given by $$\parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ , can be regarded as the “error” of using $$\mathbf{v}$$ in place of $$\textbf{y}$$ . Theorem 9 says that this error is minimized when $$\mathbf{v} = \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .

Inequality (3) leads to a new proof that $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ does not depend on the particular orthogonal basis used to compute it. If a different orthogonal basis for $$W$$ was used to construct an orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ , then this projection would also be the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ , namely $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Take $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$W$$ distinct from $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ . See Figure 4. Then $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}$$ is in $$W$$ . By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$W$$ . In particular, $$\textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is orthogonal to $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}$$ (which is in $$W$$ ). Since
$$\textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} = \left(\right. \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \left.\right) + \left(\right. \hat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \left.\right)$$
the Pythagorean Theorem gives
$$\parallel \textbf{y} - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2} = \parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2} + \parallel \hat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \parallel^{2}$$

(See the right triangle outlined in teal in Figure 4. The length of each side is labeled.) Now $$\text{∥} \widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} > 0$$ because $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} - \mathbf{v} \neq \textbf{0}$$ , and so inequality (3) follows immediately.

figure.caption: Figure 4 The orthogonal projection of y onto ﻿ W is the closest point in ﻿ W ﻿to y

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 5 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , as in Example 2, then the closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ is

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} = \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}}{\mathbf{u}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}}{\mathbf{u}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2}} \mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 2 / 5 2 1 / 5 \left]\right.$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: The distance from a point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ to a subspace $$W$$ is defined as the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to the nearest point in $$W$$ . Find the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , where
$$\textbf{y} = \left[\right. - 1 - 5 10 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{1} = \left[\right. 5 - 2 1 \left]\right. , \mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 1 2 - 1 \left]\right.$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: By the Best Approximation Theorem, the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W$$ is $$\parallel \textbf{y} - \widehat{\textbf{y}} \parallel$$ , where $$\widehat{\textbf{y}} = \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ . Since $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$W$$ ,

$$\hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \frac{15}{30} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \frac{- 21}{6} \mathbf{u}_{2} = \frac{1}{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ - 2 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \frac{7}{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 2 \\ - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 8 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 5 \\ 10\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ - 8 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{matrix} \left]\right. \parallel \textbf{y} - \hat{\textbf{y}} \parallel^{2} & = & 3^{2} + 6^{2} = 45$$
The distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to $$W$$ is $$\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$$ .

section.paragraph: The final theorem in this section shows how formula (2) for $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is simplified when the basis for $$W$$ is an orthonormal set.

note.title: Theorem ﻿10
note.heading: Theorem ﻿10
note.paragraph: If $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal basis for a subspace $$W$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Formula (4) follows immediately from (2) in Theorem 8. Also, (4) shows that $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is a linear combination of the columns of $$U$$ using the weights $$\textbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{y} \cdot \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ . The weights can be written as $$\mathbf{u}_{1}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , $$\ldots$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{p}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ , showing that they are the entries in $$U^{T}\textbf{y}$$ and justifying (5).
Suppose $$U$$ is an $$n \times p$$ matrix with orthonormal columns, and let $$W$$ be the column space of $$U$$ . Then

$$U^{T} U \textbf{x} & = & I_{p} \textbf{x} = \textbf{x} & \text{for all} \textbf{x} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{p} & \text{Theorem} 6 U U^{T} \textbf{y} & = & \text{proj} _{W} \textbf{y} & \text{for all} \textbf{y} \text{in} \mathbb{R}^{n} & \text{Theorem} 10$$

If $$U$$ is an $$n \times n$$ (square) matrix with orthonormal columns, then $$U$$ is an orthogonal matrix, the column space $$W$$ is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and $$UU^{T}\textbf{y} = I\textbf{y} = \textbf{y}$$ for all $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Although formula (4) is important for theoretical purposes, in practice it usually involves calculations with square roots of numbers (in the entries of the $$\mathbf{u}_{i}$$ ). Formula (2) is recommended for hand calculations.

Example 9 of Section 2.1 illustrates how matrix multiplication and transposition are used to detect a specified pattern illustrated using blue and white squares. Now that we have more experience working with bases for $$W$$ and $$W^{\bot}$$ , we are ready to discuss how to set up the matrix $$M$$ in Figure 6. Let $$\textbf{w}$$ be the vector generated from a pattern of blue and white squares by turning each blue square into a $$1$$ and each white square into a $$0$$ , and then lining up each column below the column before it. See Figure 5.

image.alt: A figure shows creation of a vector from colored squares.

figure.caption: Figure 5 Creating a vector from colored squares

section.paragraph: Let $$W = \text{span} \left\{ \textbf{w} \right\}$$ . Choose a basis $$\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n - 1} \right\}$$ for $$W^{\bot}$$ . Create the matrix $$B = \begin{bmatrix} {\textbf{v}_{1}}^{T} \\ {\textbf{v}_{2}}^{T} \\ \vdots \\ {\textbf{v}_{n - 1}}^{T} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Notice $$B\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ if and only if $$\textbf{u}$$ is orthogonal to a set of basis vectors for $$W^{\bot}$$ , which happens if and only if $$\textbf{u}$$ is in $$W$$ . Set $$M = B^{T}B$$ . Then $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = \textbf{u}^{T}B^{T}B\textbf{u} = {(B\textbf{u})}^{T}B\textbf{u}$$ . By Theorem 1, $${(B\textbf{u})}^{T}B\textbf{u} = 0$$ if and only if $$B\textbf{u} = 0$$ , and hence $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = 0$$ if and only if $$\textbf{u} \in W$$ . But there are only two vectors in $$W$$ consisting of zeros and ones: $$1\textbf{w} = \textbf{w}$$ and $$0\textbf{w} = \textbf{0}$$ . Thus we can conclude that if $$\textbf{u}^{T}M\textbf{u} = 0$$ , but $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{u} \neq 0$$ , then $$\textbf{u} = \textbf{w}$$ . See Figure 6.
